description: An iconic symbol and national treasure of Cambodia, the sugar palm has been beloved by people of this country for generations. Almost every part of it can be used. Fun fact: There is a famous Khmer saying about sugar palm that goes “Drop by drop, the bottle is filled”, referring to the slow drop of sweet palm sap that fills the pipe used to collect it, a process that may take half a day and requires immense patience to complete.

A favorite cultural snack eaten seasonally at the end of the dry season, the Java Plum is a fruit found on trees all across Cambodia. During the period of Khmer New Year, it is commonly eaten as a snack with dipping salts composed of salt, sugar, MSG, and chili peppers. Fun fact: Compounds in the fruit can stain your tongue purple and blue.

With blossoms often mistaken for those of strawberry plants, the Jamaican Cherry has long been another popular snack of Cambodians. The trees are resilient and can often be found by roadsides, with blooms and fruit all year round. The fruit is sweet, comparable to the taste of cotton candy or caramel, with several thousands of tiny yellow seeds inside. Fun fact: Jamaican cherries have no relation to common cherries!

khmer: ដើមចាន់រុី
description: A common source of shade from the grueling sun, the Monkey Pod also known as French Tamarind is a more rurally-found tree in Cambodia. A massive tree commonly used as a local gathering place, it can reach up to heights of 15-25 meters, with canopy diameters of up to 61 meters. Timber and shade have been the most common uses for this tree. Fun fact: it directs water to its roots by folding up its leaves at night, allowing rainwater to fall straight down.

Its most popular use being in Khmer cuisine, the jackfruit is a resilient tree that thrives best in hot, tropical climates. Being able to produce up to 200-500 fruits per year, this tree’s uses have been prevalent and diverse in Cambodia, both in traditional medicine and in local cuisines. Fun Fact: this tree is renowned for its fruit, which are considered the largest tree-born fruit in the world!

khmer: ដើមអំបែងថ្ងៃ
description: A common sight across schools in Cambodia, the Blackboard is one that has contributed largely to the country’s education. Called so because of its popular use as wood for blackboards and whiteboards, this tree symbolizes knowledge, wisdom, and protection. Despite this, it has also been feared for its size and the saccharine sweet fragrance of its flowers, which have been believed to cause hallucinations or attract malevolent spirits. Fun fact: It goes by another name: “The Devil’s Tree”.

khmer: ដើមជ្រៃស្លឹកតូច
description: Common Boxwood is a slow-growing, dense evergreen shrub native to Europe, North Africa, and Western Asia. In Cambodia, it is renowned for its ability to elevate gardens with its decorative perfection. Because of its pristine, enduring nature, boxwood is highly suitable for carving sacred iconography - such as Buddhas, devatas, and mythological creatures - allowing artisans to honor ancient Angkorian traditions in a refined, lasting way.

A common sight in Cambodia, especially in suburban or rural areas, this tree is renowned mostly for its agricultural and environmental uses. Its ability to tolerate poor soil and fix nitrogen makes it a valuable component in restoring environmental balance to degraded sites, and its light, durable wood makes it a favorite among artisans and woodworkers. Fun fact: It has an incredibly high density that makes it almost immune to dents.

A sight deeply interwoven into Southeast Asian culture and traditions, Frangipani flowers have long been revered as symbols of purity, immortality, and divinity. Many have used it as a popular offering to gods and deities, and in Cambodia, Apsara dancers have long adorned their hair with these flowers in traditional dances. Fun fact: The name Champei, which is a popular girls’ name in Cambodia, actually translates to Frangipani flower.

Renowned as the national flower of Cambodia, the Rumduol is a flower that can be found almost everywhere in the country. Predominantly found around the ancient temples of Siem Reap Province, this flower gives off a sweet scent around its blooming months (December to April). It has been featured in carvings on temple walls for centuries and serves as a vital part of Cambodian history. Fun fact: Despite being mainly known for its flowers, the Rumduol actually has fruit too!

The dwarf coconut is a variation of the species we all know and love called the coconut. Its short, stout stem and small football-like coconuts make this tree’s fruit a loved delicacy. Unlike its tall cousin, the dwarf coconut begins bearing fruit only after three or four years after planting. Its fruit contains sweet, nutrient-rich water, making it a highly valued plant, dear to the hearts of many. Fun fact: it bears fruit more quickly than its taller cousin.

A commodity among families in rural villages, this palm has become known by most in Cambodia for its popularity among old people. The areca nut is widely chewed by local families, often wrapped with betel leaves and mineral slaked lime. In Cambodian traditional medicine, the nuts and leaves are used to treat morning sickness, kill intestinal worms, and provide relief from indigestion. Fun fact: studies show that around 50% of elderly women in Cambodia chew them on the regular.

With a Khmer name that suggests that it may look like an umbrella, the Indian Almond has many uses all over Cambodia. Its leaves are prized for aquarium maintenance, while its leaves, bark, and fruit are used to create herbal teas. However, tannins from the leaves are also highly utilized for tanning leather, as well as making dyes. Fun fact: despite being a tree with multiple purposes, the Indian Almond has often not been fully used for all its purposes.

A highly valued fruit, recognizable for its vibrant, small, copious leaves alongside rich brown, nutrient-filled deliciously sour and sweet fruits. These fruits are far more than a culinary ingredient, they are a staple woven into daily life, traditional medicine, and historical heritage. Used to enhance flavor in meals, to assist digestion, and to delight the heart with delicious snacks, the Tamarind deserves a place amongst Cambodia’s most valued fruits.

Deeply embedded in Cambodian culture, the Noni makes its presence known in a variety of ways. In culinary, its leaves are a vital part of Cambodia’s national Amok dish. In traditional medicine, it is also used for general health and immunity. Its extracts have had a popular use in beauty and skincare. Fun fact: it is also often called ‘cheesefruit’ due to its pungent smell.

khmer: ដើមស្វាយប៉ោម
description: A widely recognized variety of mango, the apple mango is valued for its rich, sweet and savory taste, with a non fibrous texture that melts in a plethora of sweetness in the mouth. Highly recognized as a symbol of abundance and prosperity, the apple mango is deeply integrated into daily life, continuing to augment the Khmer culture with its sweetness. Fun Fact: The apple mango gets its name simply from its round, apple-like shape and smooth, fiberless flesh.

Blooming around April, the Golden Shower is most often seen planted around Cambodian urban or suburban areas. It is mostly used as decoration since its bright yellow flowers are said to symbolize good luck, wealth, and prosperity. Fun fact: Not many know that its seed pods, bark, leaves, and roots can also be utilized in traditional Khmer medicine.

khmer: ដើមក្រវាន់
description: This tree is a well known one that provides uses mainly in the wellness and spa industries. It has a deep, exotic, and floral scent that is soothing and thus used in massages and muscle therapy. As a result, it is also turned into perfumes or scented soaps. Fun fact: It is the main heart note of Chanel no. 5.

khmer: ដើមត្របែកព្រៃ
description: A beautiful flowering tree that comes in many colors, the Crepe Myrtle is used mostly for decorative purposes. It is planted mostly among Cambodian waterways to provide shade and attract local birds. Its water-resistant wood is also utilized in construction and traditional medicine. Fun fact: A paste made from the flowers can sometimes be applied to cuts to treat them.

This seasonal tree has three main uses in Cambodia: culinary, medical, and timber. It is often harvested from forested areas and can be eaten raw. Additionally, its leaves, roots, fruits, or seeds are widely used as a remedy to lower fevers. Its wood, specifically its branches, are a great source of firewood in rural areas. Fun fact: It bears fruit from July to September.

Known locally as milk fruit, this tree bears fruit from late January to March, during which roadside vendors can be seen popularly selling them. Its fruit tastes sweet and milky, but the latex sometimes produced from that fruit is also used, mostly as a pest repellent. Fun fact: It is named so because of the star shape its seeds and flesh produces when it is cut horizontally in half.

While a tree yielding toxic fruit and not-very-durable wood, the pong-pong tree remains one that has managed to provide some uses to Cambodians. Its seeds are used as a pest repellant, and its seeds could potentially be used in biodiesel production due to their high oil content. Fun fact: its fruit has been featured in The White Lotus.

Unfortunately a threatened resin tree species, the Hairy Leaf Apitong provides great value to Cambodia’s industries. Its wood is used in the construction of luxury goods, its bark in traditional Khmer medicine, but perhaps its most valuable use lies in its resin, which is versatile in its uses. Fun fact: that resin is known as Gurjun Balsam.

With unique green leaves that can take on a purplish tinge, the Tree Spinach is employed as a culinary and medicinal herb in Cambodia. When cooked, it takes on a flavor similar to kale or spinach. It also contains about 2-3 times as many nutrients as the regular greens. Fun fact: despite its leaves being used as an ingredient in Khmer cuisine, they are toxic when eaten raw.

khmer: ដើមរាំងភ្នំ
description: Frequently present in pagodas and other Buddhist institutions in Cambodia, this tree has long been revered as the tree under which Queen Maya, the mother of Buddha, gave birth to him. As a result, it has become a predominant symbol in Theravada Buddhism. Fun fact: The fruit is often described as having an unpleasant smell, even though the flowers are fragrant.

One of the most versatile trees in the world, bamboo can be seen utilized for many unique purposes in Cambodia. It can be eaten as shoots, crafted into artisanal goods, used in construction of footbridges and other infrastructure, and even used as transportation! Fun fact: in Battambang, there is a famous tourist attraction known as the Bamboo Lorry.

Widely grown in Cambodia, the Teak is a tree with fruit inedible to humans but makes up for it in wood. First introduced to Cambodia during a reforestation trial, its wood is highly resistant to moisture and contains no resin, making it a favorite material in kitchen utensils and luxury furniture. Fun fact: it is sometimes considered the king of wood because of its durability!

Renowned throughout the Cambodian timber industry, this tree is valued for its wood and as an environmental stabilizer. Not only is its wood durable and used often for construction, but it is also a great nitrogen fixer and soil replenisher utilized repeatedly for various community reforestation projects. Fun fact: It has deep roots that grow up to 4.5 meters deep!

Known in Southeast Asia as the freshwater mangrove, the Billabong is valued most highly for its usage in the timber and woodworking industries. In Cambodia, it is used mainly for cabinetry, interior finishes, railway carriages, and general construction. Ecologically, it also provides several benefits to the freshwater environment of Tonle Sap. Fun fact: it is also called the Indian olive!

khmer: ដើមផ្លែសេដា
description: Famous mostly for its fruit, which tastes like a dense, sweet, hard-boiled egg yolk, the Eggfruit is a seasonal fruit in Cambodia. Its fruit ripens from March to April, and it is mostly eaten as raw as a snack but can also be used to make a rich, eggnog-resembling milkshake. Fun fact: It shares a name with a popular character in Khmer literature, specifically Neang Seda from the story Reamker.

khmer: ដើមក្ងោកខ្មែរ
description: With vibrant red and orange blooms, the Royal Poinciana serves its greatest purpose in landscaping. Like many other trees in Cambodia, the Royal Poinciana has a wide canopy that provides cool shade, seasonally accompanied by vibrant blooms reminiscent of an exotic peacock’s tail. Fun fact: It is the national flower of the Caribbean Barbados Islands.

The fishtail palm (Caryota) is a striking, tropical tree native to Asia and the South Pacific. It gets its name from its uniquely shaped, jagged leaflets that closely resemble the tail fins of fish. Because of their feathery, lush appearance, they make excellent focal points for landscaping or large indoor atriums. Fun fact: they get their name from their leaflets that closely resemble the tail fin of a fish.

khmer: ដើមឆ័ត្រម៉ាឡា
description: The Madagascar almond is a beautiful tropical tree found in Madagascar, characterized by its unique layers of branches that create a well-balanced umbrella-shaped canopy. This tree is usually grown for its beauty and is an excellent shade tree, growing well in tropical areas.

khmer: ដើមអង្គារបុស្ស
description: Few trees bloom at the end of the dry season, and Millingtonia hortensis is one of them. This large tree native to Burma is recognizable by its long, tubular, white, and fragrant flowers. It usually blooms twice a year (in December and April). Its ritual function is linked to the sweet smell of its white flowers which, like those of the Frangipani, are used for sacred offerings.

khmer: ដើមអង្កាញ់
description: The Kassod is a tree with small, yellow, clustered flowers that grows at an incredible rate. Its bark and stem are used primarily to treat skin conditions, expel intestinal parasites, and reduce blood sugar levels. In foods, it can be used in curries, while in timber and woodworking, its wood is prized for its hardness and density. Additionally, it is eco-friendly, with primary uses in preventing soil erosion. Fun fact: although it can be used as food for certain animals, it is toxic to poultry and swine.

khmer: ដើមតាឡឹងតឹង
description: Found in pagodas and religious sites, the Sacred Fig, as its name suggests, is an iconic sight closely associated with Theravada Buddhism. It is the tree under which Buddha is often featured under, and per its name, represents enlightenment or supreme knowledge. Fun fact: Almost all parts of the tree can be used for medicinal purposes.

khmer: ដើមតាឡឹងតឹង
description: Prized for its fruit, the Bilimbi is a tree that thrives in the tropical climate of Southeast Asia. It is used not only as a food by acting as a natural souring agent in soups and stews, but can also be eaten raw with an iconic Cambodian mixture of pounded chilis and salt. In traditional medicine, it is used to cure coughs or colds, lower blood pressure, regulate sugar levels, and even treat acne. Fun fact: It is cauliflorous, meaning that its fruit grows directly out of its trunk and branches.

khmer: ដើមដង្កៀបក្ដាម
description: The Salamander tree is a tree whose name has evolved from the villain of old myths to a well-loved fruit. Its name stems from medieval folklore, which claims that a salamander creeping into a tree would poison all the fruit, with this tree being the victim of salamanders’ poisoning. It is often used in traditional medicines to treat diarrhea, snakebites, wounds, and relieve pain, while its fruits are eaten raw. Fun fact: It has no relation to currant shrubs, despite being also commonly called the currant tree.

khmer: ប្រេងខ្យល់
description: With a Khmer name that recognizes its significance towards the medical industry, the Rose Gum, or Flooded Gum, is another multipurpose tree. Its wood provides ‘sustainable charcoal’, while its roots help towards soil enrichment and erosion prevention, making it an environmentally sustainable tree. Moreover, essential oils extracted from the leaves are used in traditional Khmer medicine. Fun fact: It is called ‘Rose Gum’ because of the distinct light reddish-pink color of its wood.

Like most other trees in Cambodia, the Kapok is one that has multiple purposes. Its leaves are utilized as a protein-rich feed for livestock, whereas the seeds can produce oil that can then be turned into soaps. Its bark, meanwhile, is used in traditional incenses, while its unique seed pod fiber, which it is most commonly known for, is used in bedding or as stuffing. Fun fact: Because of its buoyancy, Kapok fiber was the main material used to stuff the life jackets of those aboard the Titanic.
